title: The Notification Effect

scenario.situation: An internal dashboard shows users who have notifications enabled retain at 2.4× the rate of users who don't.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The PM wants to auto-enable notifications for all new users, convinced the feature itself is driving the retention lift.
scenario.question: Does enabling notifications cause better retention, or is something else going on?

decisions.prompt: The PM is ready to ship auto-enable to 100% of new users. How do you frame the investigation before that decision?

options.label: Measure retention lift after notification delivery
options.detail: Track whether users who receive a notification in week 1 are still active in week 4.
options.consequence: You confirm that users who receive notifications are more retained — but this only holds for users who were already engaged enough to trigger a notification event. You've measured engagement predicting engagement.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the PM's hypothesis and selected on an endogenous condition.

options.label: Diagnostic segmentation by engagement level at opt-in time
options.detail: Segment users by their activity level at the moment they enabled (or never enabled) notifications, then compare retention within each activity tier.
options.consequence: Slicing by pre-opt-in engagement reveals that notification-enablers were already highly active before they ever turned the feature on. The retention gap largely disappears within matched activity tiers — the arrow may be running the other way.

options.label: A/B test notification copy and cadence
options.detail: Experiment with different notification messages to see which drives the most click-throughs.
options.consequence: You learn which copy performs best among users who opted in — but this never tests whether forcing opt-in on disengaged users improves their retention at all.
options.divergenceCost: Optimized the treatment before validating that the treatment works on the target population.

options.label: Build a retention prediction model using notification status as a feature
options.detail: Include notification-enabled as an input variable and report its coefficient as the effect.
options.consequence: The model confirms notification status is a strong predictor — because it is, as a proxy for engagement. Feature importance in an observational model cannot distinguish cause from correlation.
options.divergenceCost: Mistook predictive signal in an observational model for a causal lever.

decisions.prompt: You've segmented by pre-opt-in activity. Which metric do you use to judge whether notifications themselves drive retention?

artifact.title: 30-day retention by notification status — all new users
artifact.caption: Raw retention rates look dramatic — but enabled and disabled users differ in activity level before the opt-in decision was ever made.

options.label: Overall 30-day retention rate split by notification status
options.detail: Compare the aggregate retention of enabled vs. disabled users.
options.consequence: The 2.4× gap looks convincing, but enabled users were far more active before opt-in. You're comparing two fundamentally different populations and attributing the gap to the feature.
options.divergenceCost: Compared unadjusted groups that differ on the very thing driving the outcome.

options.label: 30-day retention rate by notification status, within matched pre-opt-in activity tiers
options.detail: Hold prior engagement constant — compare enabled vs. disabled users who had the same activity level in their first 48 hours.
options.consequence: Within each activity tier the retention gap shrinks dramatically. High-activity users retain well regardless of notification status; low-activity users retain poorly regardless. The feature explains almost none of the gap once prior engagement is controlled.

artifact.title: 30-day retention by notification status, within activity tier
artifact.caption: Within matched tiers the gap collapses to 3–5 points. Low-activity users — the auto-enable target — show almost no lift, and that small gap may still reflect residual selection.

decisions.prompt: Within activity-matched tiers, the notification retention gap nearly disappears. What do you tell the PM?

options.label: "Notifications don't drive retention — it's reverse causation. Don't ship auto-enable."
options.detail: Make the causal call and recommend killing the project.
options.consequence: You've made a confident causal claim from observational data. Matching controls for observed activity, but unmeasured factors could still confound the result. Killing the project without a randomized test leaves real value potentially on the table.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed causation from an observational analysis, even if the direction of reasoning improved.

options.label: "Engagement predicts opt-in, not the other way around — the raw gap is likely reverse causation. Run a randomized opt-in nudge experiment on low-activity users to measure the true effect before shipping to everyone."
options.detail: Present the finding, name the causal risk, and propose a randomized test to settle the direction.
options.consequence: You've reframed the PM's assumption with matched evidence, named the reverse-causation risk explicitly, and handed them a concrete next step — a randomized nudge experiment — that will produce a defensible causal answer before a costly rollout.

insight: The 2.4× retention gap was real but the causal arrow was backwards: already-engaged users self-select into enabling notifications, so notification status was a symptom of engagement, not its cause. Matching on pre-opt-in activity collapsed the gap to near zero for the very users the PM wanted to target. The lesson is reverse causation — when a behavior correlates with an outcome, ask whether the outcome is actually selecting for the behavior — and the only clean resolution is a randomized experiment that forces the variation independently of the underlying engagement.
